title: Beef Wellington
subtitle: Beef fillet wrapped in mushroom duxelles and puff pastry
excerpt: A whole beef fillet wrapped in a layer of finely chopped mushrooms, then encased in puff pastry and baked until the pastry is golden and the beef is just pink inside. The most dramatic main course in the British repertoire, and far more achievable at home than it looks.

recipe.sourceNotes: Beef Wellington is a British dish, though its exact origin is unclear; it may be named after Arthur Wellesley, the first Duke of Wellington, who supposedly enjoyed beef baked in pastry, or the name may have emerged from the shape resembling a Wellington boot. The dish became fashionable in the 1960s, partly through American adoption in high-end restaurants. The key challenge is moisture control: the mushroom mixture (duxelles) must be cooked until completely dry or the pastry will become soggy, and the beef must be seared to form a dry crust before wrapping. The internal temperature at serving is critical: 52 to 54°C for medium-rare. Using a thermometer is essential.

recipeTools.notes: Essential for hitting the correct internal temperature. Pull the Wellington at 52°C; it will rise to 54 to 55°C during resting.

content.text: The duxelles must be cooked until completely dry, with no moisture remaining in the pan. Any wetness will turn the pastry base soggy. The beef must rest after searing and again after baking. Wrap the assembled Wellington tightly in cling film and chill for at least 30 minutes before baking so it holds its shape.

items.preparation: very finely chopped or blended to a paste

content.text: Season the beef well. Heat the oil in a frying pan over the highest heat. Sear the fillet on all sides for a total of 3 to 4 minutes until deeply browned all over. Brush immediately with Dijon mustard. Leave to cool completely.

Cook the shallot in butter until soft. Add the mushroom paste and garlic. Cook over high heat, stirring constantly, for 10 to 15 minutes until all the moisture has evaporated and the mixture is completely dry. Season and add the thyme. Cool completely.

Lay a large sheet of cling film on the work surface. Spread the cold duxelles over it in a rectangle large enough to wrap the beef. Lay the beef at the edge nearest you and roll tightly into a cylinder using the cling film. Twist the ends and refrigerate for 30 minutes.

Heat the oven to 220°C / fan 200°C / gas 7. Roll out 500 g ready-made puff pastry. Unwrap the beef and place at the edge. Roll tightly into a parcel, sealing the join and ends with egg wash. Brush all over with egg wash. Score lightly. Chill for 15 minutes. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the pastry is golden and the internal temperature reads 52°C. Rest for 10 minutes before slicing.
